plan.summary: Budget concentrates on Movewell, the one large publisher whose checkout carries explicit training intent, with tests on Studiogrid (fitness bookings), Cloudfoot (activewear) and a capped test on Swiftcart's impulse-friendly young male-leaning scale; Daily Form is excluded as a supplements competitor and the wellness-grocery/beverage placements are dropped because their clean-label, indulgence sensibilities clash with a performance-only, price-first pitch.

recommended.name: Movewell
recommended.tier_reason: The score treated this as a generic apparel/audience match, but the notes name the exact intent this brand needs: these shoppers train, and someone who just bought activewear is a natural buyer of protein and creatine. A $40 supplement order against a $78 activewear basket is an easy add-on, and 22M impressions is the largest genuinely fitness-intent inventory here.
recommended.rationale: Notes describe "Fitness-engaged shoppers" buying activewear, so a value-priced protein/creatine offer lands seconds after a training-related purchase at roughly half the basket size.
recommended.risk: 82% female and a strong beauty/wellness crossover means much of this traffic may be athleisure buyers rather than gym-goers, and pre-workout/creatine skews male.

test.name: Studiogrid
test.rationale: Shoppers here have just booked a class or personal training session, which is the closest thing to a declared training habit, and $40 matches the $42 typical booking spend.

evidence.quote: Users are actively spending on self-care and fitness

test.risk: The spa/yoga half of this inventory is self-care rather than performance training, and a high-income audience is the least moved by "half the cost" positioning; worth measuring class type against conversion.

test.name: Swiftcart
test.tier_reason: Excluded as off-category, but this is the one place where the shopper profile matches the product's core buyer and the offer mechanics: 18-34, male-leaning, mid income, impulse-friendly, at 84M impressions, with a $40 offer against a $28 basket.
test.rationale: Notes call the traffic "High-frequency purchasers" and "Impulse-friendly" among an 18-34, 51% male mid-income base, the demographic core of budget pre-workout and creatine; worth a capped test purely on scale and price alignment.

evidence.quote: High-frequency purchasers. Late-night traffic spike. Impulse-friendly

test.risk: No fitness intent at all in the basket (groceries, alcohol, household), and convenience-delivery shoppers self-select for paying up for speed, not for hunting the cheapest formulation.

test.name: Cloudfoot
test.rationale: Activewear and shoes for a 25-45 audience with a near-even gender split is plausible training traffic, and $40 is small against a $118 basket.

evidence.quote: Tech-adjacent urban professionals. Comfort + sustainability messaging

test.risk: Comfort and sustainability messaging suggests everyday lifestyle footwear buyers rather than gym-goers, and 5.8M impressions limits how fast a read comes in.

launch_summary.summary: $8,500 of the $10,000 goes to Movewell, the one large publisher whose checkout shows explicit training intent, running all four personas from The Fitness Enthusiast to The Busy Parent. The remaining $1,500 is split evenly across three tests: Studiogrid (class and training bookings), Cloudfoot (activewear) and Swiftcart, where only The Fitness Enthusiast ad runs and the basket shows no fitness intent. Each test asks whether that traffic converts at or below the $12.00 target within 14 days.
uncertainties: The $40 first order value is assumed, and the $12.00 target and $15.60 maximum cost per new customer are built directly on it.
Purchases are assumed to be one-time with no subscription, so the first order alone has to pay back acquisition; real repeat behaviour would change what you can afford to pay.
Swiftcart's shoppers self-select for paying up for convenience rather than hunting the cheapest formulation, and Cloudfoot's 5.8M impressions may be too few for a fast read.
questions: What is your actual average first order value, and your margin on it?
Do customers resubscribe or reorder, and how often?
Is the 20-45 any-gender audience right, or does your buyer base skew male?
